# General discussion

\OnehalfSpacing

<!-- The future of our oceans depend on the amount of anthropogenic carbon emitted in the next few decades. -->

<!-- The era of the Anthropocene continues to stress our climate system worldwide, and these changes are causing deterioration of our marine ecosystems at an unprecedented scales, from mass mortality events to the redistribution of marine biodiversity, all compounded by the threat of increased extreme events [@Hughes2017a; @Harris2018; @Sommer2018]. -->
A significant challenge in this era of the Anthropocene is to improve our predictive power with regards to the ecologically important outcomes of climate change. 
These impacts on the ocean are multi-faceted, with strong synergies between abiotic stressors (e.g. temperature and pH) shaped by regional patterns of variability in time and space. 
Addressing the influence of these interaction are vital to predicting the resilience of marine communities to environmental change [@Boyd2015; @Lange2017].
However, it is also important to understand the basic physiological mechanisms influencing the responses of marine organisms to these stressors, of which temperature is a fundamental driver [@Somero2017; @Pettersen2018].
To accomplish this, it is key to integrate single species, ecophysiological approaches to test hypotheses involving multiple stressors, changing abiotic conditions and phenotypic plasticity. 
It is also important that methods are easily reproducible so that the research in the field can progress through time and replication. 

This thesis addresses the knowledge gaps above, and although the long-term and multi-stressor experimental methods were applied to a single species of sea urchin, the outcomes are relevant to current and future predictions of resilience of other taxa to our increasingly altered ocean.
Importantly, this thesis shows evidence that the future will pose considerable challenges to the resilience of this sea urchin (and similar taxa), the outcomes of this thesis highlight the fact that that in addition to phenotypic plasticity, trans-generational effects (e.g. transgenerational plasticity and developmental plasticity) and genetic adaptation will also play major roles in the alteration of species occurrences and performances under climate change.
<!-- The results of  experiments highlighted the importance of temperature, and the interactive influence (from a multistressor context) of low pH, on the physiologicsl responses of *H. erythrogramma*. -->


## Timing affects stress responses

<!-- To be ecologically relevant, experiments that aim to determine the stress responses of an organism to environmental stressors must first consider the spatial and temporal nature of the natural environment that the organism occupies. -->
All adult acclimation experiments in this thesis (Chapters \@ref(chapter2) to \@ref(chapter4)) were performed with careful consideration of the natural environment inhabited by *H. erythrogramma*.
<!-- Temperature levels were determined based on in situ loggers deployed at collection sites, and  -->
The first study (Chapter \@ref(chapter2)) used the annual mean temperature of the sea urchin habitat in Sydney Harbour to establish constant temeprature treatments and determine thermal limits.
Subsequent studies (Chapters \@ref(chapter3), \@ref(chapter4)) incorporated a baseline representation of temperature conditions with weekly adjustments, based on logger data to reflect the realistic pattern of seasonal change experienced by the sea urchins.
These considerations were critical in disentangling the chronic effects of envrionmental stress on the physiological responses of *H. erythrogramma*. 
The results of Chapter \@ref(chapter2) showed that the upper thermal tolerance limit of *H. erythrogramma* was 26 \degree C, however Chapter \@ref(chapter3) also showed that significant mortality can occur at lower temperature levels (20 \degree C to 25 \degree C) when temperature levels followed the long-term seasonal trend between winter and summer.
The results underline the vital importance of seasonal dynamics on organismal responses, and the consequences of exposure to climate change stressors depend critically on the timing of introduction of stressors.

The inclusion of seasonality of temperature is rarely taken into account as most studies use constant temperature to establish their conditions []

## Linking physiology to resilience

For adult *H. erythrogramma*, warming appears to be the dominant stressor affecting all physiological responses significantly.

## Future directions

There is no doubt that climate change will alter marine biodiversity in the future [@Hillebrand2018]. The work presented in this thesis provides an experimental framework with which to undertake climate change research utilising multiple stressors
